Analytical Provisioning for Attention–FFN Disaggregated LLM Serving under Stochastic Workloads

Chendong Song ††thanks: Corresponding author: songcd@ust.hk Affiliation: Dept. of Industrial Engineering Affiliation: and Decision Analytics Affiliation: HKUST, Hong Kong, China    Meixuan Wang Affiliation: Huawei Hong Kong Affiliation: Research Center, China    Hang Zhou Affiliation: Dept. of Industrial Engineering Affiliation: and Decision Analytics Affiliation: HKUST, Hong Kong, China    Hong Liang Affiliation: Huawei Hong Kong Affiliation: Research Center, China    Yuan Lyu Affiliation: Huawei Hong Kong Affiliation: Research Center, China    Zixi Chen Affiliation: Huawei Hong Kong Affiliation: Research Center, China    Yuwei Fan Affiliation: Huawei Hong Kong Affiliation: Research Center, China    Zijie Zhou ††thanks: Corresponding author: jerryzhou@ust.hk Affiliation: Dept. of Industrial Engineering Affiliation: and Decision Analytics Affiliation: HKUST, Hong Kong, China
Abstract

Attention–FFN disaggregation (AFD) is an emerging architecture for LLM decoding that separates state-heavy, KV-cache–dominated Attention computation from stateless, compute-intensive FFN computation, connected by per-step communication. While AFD enables independent scaling of memory and compute resources, its performance is highly sensitive to the Attention/FFN provisioning ratio: mis-sizing induces step-level blocking and costly device idle time. We develop an analytical provisioning framework for AFD bundles in an rrA–11F topology under stochastic workloads. Two sources of randomness shape the problem: per-slot Attention workload evolves as KV caches grow and completed requests are replenished with random prompt and decode lengths, and synchronized execution across Attention workers introduces a barrier governed by the slowest worker. We address both via a renewal-reward characterization of the per-slot stationary token load, identifying a single workload statistic θ\theta that governs provisioning under arbitrary prefill-decode distributions and admits a nonparametric estimator from request traces. The analysis yields a closed-form mean-field rule for the optimal A/F ratio decomposing into Attention-, communication-, and FFN-bottleneck regimes, together with a Gaussian barrier-aware refinement that quantifies cross-worker synchronization overhead. A trace-calibrated AFD simulator supports the framework across workloads: the predicted optimal ratio matches the simulation-optimal within 10%. Together, these results provide a compact, calibratable account of how stochastic workload structure determines provisioning in disaggregated LLM serving.

1 Introduction

The explosive growth of large language models (LLMs) (Brown et al., 2020; Chowdhery et al., 2023; OpenAI, 2023; Kaplan et al., 2020) has created unprecedented challenges for efficient inference serving at scale. As model sizes expand into hundreds of billions of parameters, modern LLM serving inevitably requires distributed multi-device architectures. This reality has spurred a shift from monolithic serving paradigms toward increasingly sophisticated disaggregation strategies that decompose the inference pipeline across heterogeneous hardware resources.

Early efforts of disaggregate serving focused on stage-level separation, exemplified by the Prefill-Decode (PD) disaggregation (Zhong et al., 2024; Patel et al., 2024). LLM inference comprises two phases with distinct resource profiles: prefill processes the input prompt and generates the KV cache via dense matrix operations (compute-bound), while decode generates tokens autoregressively, reading the accumulated KV cache at each step (memory-bound). PD disaggregation separates these phases onto hardware matched to their respective bottlenecks. By disaggregating prefill and decode onto separate hardware pools that can be independently scaled, PD architectures enable higher decode batch sizes through request aggregation, improving GPU utilization during token generation.

Building upon this foundation, recent research has recognized that even within the decode phase, computational heterogeneity persists between different transformer components. The Attention-FFN Decoupling (AFD) (Wang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Zuo et al., 2025) extends this disaggregation further: Attention layers are stateful and memory-bound (dominated by KV cache reads), whereas FFN layers are stateless and can achieve compute-bound operation with sufficient batching. Traditional coupled architectures often leave FFN compute units underutilized due to the small decode batch with TPOT constraints. AFD architecture strategically disaggregates these components, allowing multiple Attention instances to feed into an aggregated FFN instances. This topology maximizes FFN arithmetic intensity while independently scaling memory resources for Attention.

Recent work (Wang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Zuo et al., 2025) has shown that AFD can significantly improve serving efficiency by allowing Attention and FFN to scale independently. Given this flexibility, a central design decision in such systems is the ratio of Attention instances to FFN instances, which we denote as rr. Currently, existing systems set rr through empirical search or naive deterministic approximations that ignore workload stochasticity. A principled analytical provisioning framework is still lacking. This gap matters because the choice of rr directly impacts system efficiency: when rr is too small, the FFN server starves for input; when rr is too large, Attention instances block waiting for FFN availability.

Finding a principled analytical provisioning rule, however, is non-trivial because the Attention workload is fundamentally stochastic. FFN computation depends only on batch size and remains stable across decode steps. In contrast, Attention workload evolves continuously—the KV cache grows with each step, and completed requests are replaced by new ones with variable prompt lengths.

As AFD remains an emerging paradigm with no mature open-source implementations, principled analytical foundations are needed to guide this design space before extensive system building begins. In this paper, we provide such foundations through a rigorous probabilistic framework that captures the stochastic dynamics of Attention-side workload and derives a closed-form expression for the optimal A/F ratio. Our simulation-based validation demonstrates that the theory accurately predicts system behavior; real-system validation is left to future work as AFD implementations mature. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

(i) Probabilistic workload model. We develop an analytical framework capturing the stochastic dynamics of AFD serving under continuous batching with request replenishment. Using a discrete-time renewal-reward analysis of one decode slot, we identify a single workload statistic that governs provisioning under arbitrary prompt and decode-length distributions and admits a nonparametric estimator from request traces.

(ii) Provisioning rule with load-balancing correction. We derive a closed-form mean-field rule for the A/F ratio that decomposes into three operating regimes (Attention-bottleneck, communication-bottleneck, FFN-bottleneck), each with an interpretable balance condition. Cross-worker synchronization stragglers are handled via a Gaussian order-statistic correction.

(iii) Validation across workloads and hardware regimes. We develop a trace-calibrated AFD simulator and validate the framework across diverse workload and hardware configurations. The closed-form rule matches the simulator-optimal ratio within 10%, which is an empirical confirmation of the theory.

2 Background on Attention-FFN Disaggregation: Pipeline and Microbatch

In standard LLM decoding, a monolithic architecture deploys both Attention and FFN blocks on the same hardware. To reduce kernel launch overhead and execution bubbles, practitioners typically compile the model into a static execution graph (e.g., CUDA Graphs (Ekelund et al., 2025)), which enforces fixed batch sizes across all components. This rigidity creates a utilization problem: time per output token (TPOT) latency constraints force small batch sizes, and at low concurrency, FFN blocks cannot amortize their weight-loading cost—despite being computationally dense, they become memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute-bound.

AFD addresses this by disaggregating Attention and FFN onto separate hardware, enabling an asymmetric r:1r:1 deployment where multiple Attention instances feed a shared FFN server. We now describe the execution mechanics of this architecture.

In an AF-disaggregated deployment, each Transformer layer comprises three distinct stages: Attention computation, FFN computation, and inter-device Communication (A↔FA\leftrightarrow F). As illustrated in Figure 1, Attention blocks are stateful: during each decode step, every continuing request generates one output token, and its corresponding key-value is appended to the KV cache. When computing attention, the model must read the entire accumulated KV cache for each request, so the Attention cost grows linearly with sequence length. When a request completes, its slot is immediately refilled with a newly prefill request to maintain batch size (continuous batching). In contrast, FFN blocks are stateless—their computation depends only on the current activations, not on sequence history. To handle the latency introduced by transferring activations (AF communication) across LL layers within one decode step, microbatch pipelining is adopted, as shown in Figure 2.

Figure 2(a) depicts an ideal execution schedule. Here, Am​nA_{mn}, Cm​nC_{mn}, and Fm​nF_{mn} denote Attention, Communication, and FFN operations for the nn-th microbatch at the mm-th layer, respectively. With sufficient microbatches (typically ≥3\geq 3), the system overlaps Communication and FFN of one microbatch with Attention of subsequent microbatches, thereby masking data transfer (communication) latency.

However, Attention’s stateful nature introduces dynamic variability that disrupts this ideal schedule. Consider Figure 2(b): after one decode step, assuming no request completes, every request’s KV cache has grown by one token. Consequently, A11A_{11}, A12A_{12}, and A13A_{13} all take longer than in the previous step, while Cm​nC_{mn} and Fm​nF_{mn} remain unchanged. The increased Attention time means that A12A_{12} and A13A_{13} can no longer fit in the gaps between layers—A13A_{13} is deferred, leaving idle “bubbles" in the pipeline. Depending on the workload imbalance, bubbles may appear on the Attention side (waiting for FFN) or the FFN side (starved of data from Attention). Since Attention workload drifts continuously, no static microbatch schedule remains ideal over time. This motivates our central question: how to determine the optimal Attention-to-FFN ratio (rr:1) that minimizes expected pipeline bubbles across a long serving horizon.

3 Mathematical Model

We consider an AFD bundle in a general xxA–yyF topology, where xx Attention instances feed into yy shared FFN instances. To simplify notation, we define the Attention-to-FFN ratio r:=x/yr:=x/y and express the topology equivalently as rrA–11F. rr does not need to be an integer, for example, r=3.5r=3.5 corresponds to a 77A–22F configuration. Each Attention instance maintains a microbatch of BB requests and their associated KV caches. Decoding proceeds in synchronized steps, where each step comprises four phases:

  1. (i)

    Attention phase: The rr Attention workers execute in parallel, each processing its microbatch of BB requests (total r​BrB requests across the bundle).

  2. (ii)

    A→\toF communication: All rr Attention workers transfer their intermediate activations to the shared FFN worker.

  3. (iii)

    FFN phase: The FFN worker processes the aggregated batch of r​BrB activations.

  4. (iv)

    F→\toA communication: The FFN worker returns outputs to all rr Attention workers.

Our goal is to determine the optimal ratio r∗r^{*} that maximizes system throughput.

3.1 Latency Models

We adopt linear latency models grounded in first-principles hardware analysis (see Appendix B for detailed derivations) and consistent with established results in the LLM inference literature.

Attention. The Attention computation reads the KV cache for all requests in the microbatch. For a microbatch of BB requests, let sbs_{b} denote the prefill length and ibi_{b} the current decode index for request bb. The total token load is T=∑b=1B(sb+ib)T=\sum_{b=1}^{B}(s_{b}+i_{b}). During decoding, Attention is memory-bandwidth bound—dominated by reading the KV cache from HBM (Kwon et al., 2023; Pope et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2024). By the roofline model, latency for a memory-bound operation equals data volume divided by effective bandwidth (Yuan et al., 2024; Lienhart, 2024), so Attention latency scales linearly with TT: tA​(T)=αA​T+βAt_{A}(T)=\alpha_{A}T+\beta_{A}.

FFN. The FFN processes batched activations and becomes compute-bound with sufficient batching (Agrawal et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2024). FFN layers perform matrix multiplications whose FLOPs scale as O⁡(batch×hidden×intermediate)O(\text{batch}\times\text{hidden}\times\text{intermediate}), yielding linear latency in batch size (Pope et al., 2023; Chen, 2023): tF​(r​B)=αF​(r​B)+βFt_{F}(rB)=\alpha_{F}(rB)+\beta_{F}.

Communication. The round-trip communication cost per Attention instance is tC​(r​B)=αC​(r​B)+βCt_{C}(rB)=\alpha_{C}(rB)+\beta_{C}, where βC\beta_{C} is a fixed startup cost and αC​(r​B)\alpha_{C}(rB) is the bandwidth-dependent term. This is the standard model for distributed communication, validated extensively in GPU clusters (Narayanan et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024).

3.2 Workload Characterization

Request lengths. Each request has a prefill length P∈ℤ≥0P\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} and a decode lifetime D∈{1,2,…}D\in\{1,2,\ldots\}, where DD is the number of decode steps the request occupies its slot. During those DD steps, the decode index takes values 0,1,…,D−10,1,\ldots,D-1. We treat (Pn,Dn)n≥1(P_{n},D_{n})_{n\geq 1} as i.i.d. across requests, allowing arbitrary dependence between PnP_{n} and DnD_{n} within a request. We assume only that 𝔼⁡[P]\mathbb{E}[P], 𝔼⁡[D]\mathbb{E}[D], and the second moment of the per-slot stationary load (defined in Section 4.1) are finite. No specific distributional family is required.

Continuous batching. Following standard practice in LLM serving, we use continuous batching: whenever a request completes, its slot is immediately refilled with a new request from the queue, maintaining full microbatches throughout serving.

Cross-worker load balancing. The rr Attention workers in a bundle execute synchronously, so the Attention phase waits for the slowest worker. Stochastic request dynamics induce heterogeneous token loads across workers, creating a straggler effect that grows with rr. Implementing load-balancing routing policies (Chen et al., 2026) can mitigate this gap, though some irreducible variance from stochastic dynamics remains.

3.3 Optimization Objective

Cycle time. Let TjT_{j} denote the total token load on Attention worker j∈{1,…,r}j\in\{1,\ldots,r\}. Because the rr workers execute synchronously, the Attention phase completes only when the slowest worker finishes. The relevant Attention-side load is therefore the barrier load WB,r:=max1≤j≤r⁡TjW_{B,r}:=\max_{1\leq j\leq r}T_{j}. The per-step cycle time is τ⁡(B,r)=max⁡{αA​WB,r+βA,tC​(r​B),tF​(r​B)}\tau(B;r)=\max\big\{\alpha_{A}W_{B,r}+\beta_{A},\;t_{C}(rB),\;t_{F}(rB)\big\}.

Throughput per instance. Long-run throughput is governed by the expected cycle time τ¯​(B,r):=𝔼⁡[τ⁡(B,r)]\bar{\tau}(B;r):=\mathbb{E}[\tau(B;r)]. We maximize the average number of output tokens generated per unit time, normalized by the total number of instances (rr Attention ++ 11 FFN):

Throughputper​-​inst​(B,r)=1r+1⋅r​Bτ¯​(B,r),\mathrm{Throughput}_{\mathrm{per\text{-}inst}}(B;r)=\frac{1}{r+1}\cdot\frac{rB}{\bar{\tau}(B;r)}, (1)

where r​BrB is the number of tokens generated per cycle across the bundle.

The central challenge is that τ¯​(B,r)\bar{\tau}(B;r) is shaped by two sources of stochasticity. Within each Attention worker, per-slot loads evolve as decoding progresses and slots are replenished with random prompt and decode lengths, so the workload is non-stationary at the step level even though it admits a stationary distribution under continuous batching. Across workers, the maximum in WB,rW_{B,r} introduces a synchronization barrier whose expected overhead grows with rr. The next section develops a probabilistic analysis to provide a provisioning rule.

4 Analysis and Optimal A/F Ratio

We now derive the optimal Attention-to-FFN ratio r∗r^{*}. The analysis must contend with two sources of randomness simultaneously: per-slot Attention workload evolves pathwise as decoding progresses, with KV caches growing and completed slots replenished by new requests of random length, and the synchronized Attention phase is governed by a barrier across the rr workers. Classical fork-join queueing models assume stationary, identical service times and therefore do not directly apply. We address both effects by combining a renewal-reward characterization of the per-slot stationary load with a Gaussian order-statistic correction for the cross-worker barrier. The analysis yields a closed-form mean-field provisioning rule, refined by a barrier-aware correction that captures synchronization overhead.

4.1 Stationary Per-Slot Token Load

By symmetry, it suffices to analyze one decode slot under continuous batching. Requests arrive at the slot sequentially. Request nn has prompt length Pn∈ℤ≥0P_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} and decode lifetime Dn∈{1,2,…}D_{n}\in\{1,2,\ldots\}, with (Pn,Dn)n≥1(P_{n},D_{n})_{n\geq 1} i.i.d. across requests. During its lifetime, the request occupies the slot for DnD_{n} decode steps, contributing token load Pn+aP_{n}+a at age a∈{0,1,…,Dn−1}a\in\{0,1,\ldots,D_{n}-1\}. Let YY denote the stationary token load of one slot, observed at a uniformly random decode step, and define θ:=𝔼⁡[Y]\theta:=\mathbb{E}[Y], ν2:=Var⁡(Y)\nu^{2}:=\mathrm{Var}(Y).

Lemma 4.1 (Stationary token-load moments).

Assume 0<𝔼⁡[D]<∞0<\mathbb{E}[D]<\infty and

𝔼⁡[D​P2+P​D​(D−1)+D​(D−1)​(2​D−1)6]<∞.\mathbb{E}\!\left[DP^{2}+PD(D-1)+\tfrac{D(D-1)(2D-1)}{6}\right]<\infty. (2)

Then

θ=𝔼⁡[D​P+D⁡(D−1)2]𝔼⁡[D],𝔼⁡[Y2]=𝔼⁡[D​P2+P​D​(D−1)+D​(D−1)​(2​D−1)6]𝔼⁡[D],\theta=\frac{\mathbb{E}\!\left[DP+\tfrac{D(D-1)}{2}\right]}{\mathbb{E}[D]},\qquad\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]=\frac{\mathbb{E}\!\left[DP^{2}+PD(D-1)+\tfrac{D(D-1)(2D-1)}{6}\right]}{\mathbb{E}[D]}, (3)

and ν2=𝔼⁡[Y2]−θ2\nu^{2}=\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]-\theta^{2}. If PP and DD are independent,

θ=μP+μD−12+σD22​μD,\theta=\mu_{P}+\frac{\mu_{D}-1}{2}+\frac{\sigma_{D}^{2}}{2\mu_{D}}, (4)

where μD:=𝔼⁡[D]\mu_{D}:=\mathbb{E}[D] and σD2:=Var⁡(D)\sigma_{D}^{2}:=\mathrm{Var}(D). Without independence, an additional term Cov⁡(P,D)/μD\mathrm{Cov}(P,D)/\mu_{D} enters.

The proof, given in Appendix A.1, applies the discrete-time renewal-reward theorem to one decode slot, treating each request as a renewal cycle of length DnD_{n}.

Equation (4) identifies the workload statistic that drives provisioning: it is not the arrival-average μP+μD\mu_{P}+\mu_{D} (a natural but incorrect first guess), but the stationary age-adjusted load. The decode-length variance σD2\sigma_{D}^{2} enters through length-biasing (longer requests are sampled more often when observed at a random decode step) and the prefill–decode covariance enters when long prompts induce long responses. The framework imposes no parametric assumption on (P,D)(P,D); Appendix A.6 gives a nonparametric estimator that calibrates θ\theta and ν2\nu^{2} directly from request traces.

Remark 4.2 (Bounded request lengths).

In practice, serving systems impose maximum context and generation lengths, so PP and DD are bounded and condition (2) is automatically satisfied. Appendix A.7 discusses the role of length-biasing under unbounded distributions for completeness.

Each Attention worker j∈{1,…,r}j\in\{1,\ldots,r\} holds BB slots with stationary loads Yj,bY_{j,b}, i.i.d. across (j,b)(j,b). 4.4 Provisioning Rules

We present a closed-form mean-field rule and a barrier-aware refinement.

Theorem 4.4 (Mean-field optimal A/F ratio).

Under the mean-field cycle time (8), the throughput is maximized by evaluating the following candidate ratios:

r∗mf∈{min{μA−βCαC​B,μA−βFαF​B},βCαC​B,βFαF​B,βC−βFB⁡(αF−αC)}.\boxed{\begin{gathered}\displaystyle r^{*}_{\mathrm{mf}}\in\Bigg\{\min\!\left\{\frac{\mu_{A}-\beta_{C}}{\alpha_{C}B},\frac{\mu_{A}-\beta_{F}}{\alpha_{F}B}\right\},\quad\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{C}}{\alpha_{C}B}},\quad\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{F}}{\alpha_{F}B}},\quad\frac{\beta_{C}-\beta_{F}}{B(\alpha_{F}-\alpha_{C})}\Bigg\}.\end{gathered}} (10)

Throughputmf∗=rmf∗​B(rmf∗+1)​τmf​(B,rmf∗).\mathrm{Throughput}^{*}_{\mathrm{mf}}=\frac{r^{*}_{\mathrm{mf}}B}{(r^{*}_{\mathrm{mf}}+1)\tau_{\mathrm{mf}}(B;r^{*}_{\mathrm{mf}})}.

The proof is in Appendix A.5. Since communication and FFN both scale with the aggregate batch r​BrB, communication enters through τmf\tau_{\mathrm{mf}} directly, rather than through a separate θ\theta-dependent balance term. Barrier-aware refinement. When the cross-worker barrier is retained, the throughput

ThrG​(B,r):=r​B(r+1)​τG​(B,r)\mathrm{Thr}_{G}(B;r):=\frac{rB}{(r+1)\,\tau_{G}(B;r)} (11)

is no longer maximized in closed form, because τG​(B,r)\tau_{G}(B;r) depends on rr both through the FFN term αF​r​B+βF\alpha_{F}rB+\beta_{F} in GB,rG_{B,r} and through the order-statistic factor κr∼2​log⁡r\kappa_{r}\sim\sqrt{2\log r} inside the integral. The barrier-aware optimal ratio is

rG∗∈arg⁡maxr∈ℛ​ThrG​(B,r),\boxed{\,r^{*}_{G}\in\arg\max_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\mathrm{Thr}_{G}(B;r),\,} (12)

where ℛ\mathcal{R} is the feasible set of integer fan-ins. This is a one-dimensional analytic optimization evaluable in milliseconds combined with a discrete search over rr. In the practically common setting where decode lengths approximately follow a geometric distribution—as observed across multiple production LLM traces (Figure 5 in Appendix A.8)—the moment statistics admit closed-form expressions, yielding the following specialization.

Corollary 4.5 (Geometric decode lifetimes).

If PP and DD are independent and D∼Geom⁡(p)D\sim\mathrm{Geom}(p) on {1,2,…}\{1,2,\ldots\}, write μout:=(1−p)/p\mu_{\mathrm{out}}:=(1-p)/p for the expected number of generated tokens. Then

θ=μP+μout,ν2=σP2+μout​(μout+1),\theta=\mu_{P}+\mu_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad\nu^{2}=\sigma_{P}^{2}+\mu_{\mathrm{out}}(\mu_{\mathrm{out}}+1),

so the mean-field rule (10) reduces to the form derived in prior analyses of LLM decoding under geometric assumptions, while (12) sharpens it with the synchronization correction.

Practical recipe. Given hardware parameters (αA,βA,αF,βF,αC,βC)(\alpha_{A},\beta_{A},\alpha_{F},\beta_{F},\alpha_{C},\beta_{C}) and request traces (Pi,Di)i=1n(P_{i},D_{i})_{i=1}^{n}: (i) Estimate θ^\hat{\theta} and ν^2\hat{\nu}^{2} from the trace using the nonparametric estimator (Appendix A.6). (ii) Compute rmf∗r^{*}_{\mathrm{mf}} in closed form via Theorem 4.4 as a fast initial recommendation. (iii) Refine via rG∗r^{*}_{G} from (12) when cross-worker imbalance is non-negligible.

5 Numerical Experiments

To validate our theoretical framework, we develop an AFD simulator and conduct systematic experiments comparing theoretical predictions with simulation results. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AF-release-1C11.

5.1 Simulator Design

The simulator implements a discrete-event, cycle-by-cycle simulation of the rrA–11F topology, where each Batch object transitions through a six-state finite state machine (Attention →\to A2F transfer →\to Waiting →\to FFN →\to F2A transfer →\to Waiting →\to repeat). To maximize resource utilization, the simulator maintains two batches in flight simultaneously: while one batch is being processed by the shared FFN server, the Attention instances process the other batch in parallel, and vice versa. This interleaved execution allows computation on one batch to overlap with communication and processing of the other, effectively hiding transfer latencies.

5.2 Experimental Setup

Latency parameters and configuration. We adopt linear latency coefficients calibrated for the DeepSeek-V3 architecture deployed on Huawei Ascend 910C NPUs, obtained via linear regression on real execution traces: αA=0.00165\alpha_{A}=0.00165 cycles/token, βA=50\beta_{A}=50 cycles, αF=0.083\alpha_{F}=0.083 cycles/request, βF=100\beta_{F}=100 cycles, αC=0.022\alpha_{C}=0.022 cycles/token, and βC=20\beta_{C}=20 cycles. Appendix B provides the general derivation framework, enabling practitioners to calibrate these parameters for other hardware platforms. Under this configuration, communication latency can be effectively hidden through pipelining (tA,tF>2​tCt_{A},t_{F}>2t_{C} across operating regimes), so our analysis focuses on balancing Attention and FFN workloads. We fix batch size B=256B=256, expected decode length μD=500\mu_{D}=500 (σD2=294500\sigma_{D}^{2}=294500) tokens, and expected prefill length μP=100\mu_{P}=100 (σP2=9900\sigma_{P}^{2}=9900) tokens. We sweep r∈{1,2,4,8,16,24,32}r\in\{1,2,4,8,16,24,32\} and simulate until N=10,000N=10{,}000 requests complete per Attention instance. By Theorem 4.4, The theoretical optimal A/F ratio is: rmf∗≈9.3r^{*}_{\mathrm{mf}}\approx 9.3.

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate the following metrics to assess system performance:

  • •

    Stable Throughput per Instance: To avoid distortion from startup transients and tail effects (e.g., the final requests draining with partially filled batches), we report throughput computed over the first 80% of completed requests. Specifically, we measure T80%T_{80\%} as the time when ⌈0.8​N⌉\lceil 0.8N\rceil requests have completed, and compute Throughputper-inst(80%)=1r+1⋅∑i=1⌈0.8​N⌉DiT80%,\text{Throughput}_{\text{per-inst}}^{(80\%)}=\frac{1}{r+1}\cdot\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\lceil 0.8N\rceil}D_{i}}{T_{80\%}}, where DiD_{i} is the number of output tokens generated for the ii-th request.

  • •

    Time Per Output Token (TPOT): The average time to generate a single output token per request, defined as TPOT=1N​∑i=1NTdecode(i)Di,\text{TPOT}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{T_{\text{decode}}^{(i)}}{D_{i}}, where Tdecode(i)T_{\text{decode}}^{(i)} denotes the total decode time for the ii-th request.

  • •

    Idle Ratios: To quantify resource utilization, we measure the fraction of time that each component remains idle waiting for synchronization: ηA=1r​∑i=1rtidle,A(i)Ttotal\eta_{A}=\frac{1}{r}\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{t_{\text{idle},A}^{(i)}}{T_{\text{total}}}, ηF=tidle,FTtotal\eta_{F}=\frac{t_{\text{idle},F}}{T_{\text{total}}}, where tidle,A(i)t_{\text{idle},A}^{(i)} and tidle,Ft_{\text{idle},F} denote the total idle waiting time of the ii-th Attention instance and the shared FFN instance, respectively. Lower values indicate better utilization; in an ideally balanced system, both ηA,ηF→0\eta_{A},\eta_{F}\to 0.

5.3 Results

Figure 3 shows per-instance throughput, TPOT, and idle ratios as functions of rr. The theoretical optimal rmf∗≈9.3r^{*}_{\mathrm{mf}}\approx 9.3 closely matches the simulation-optimal ratio. Moreover, the theoretical throughput curve tracks the simulation results well across all configurations, validating our analytical framework. A residual gap of up to ∼15%{\sim}15\% between the mean-field prediction and simulation emerges at large rr, consistent with the barrier-aware analysis in Section 4.2: the synchronization overhead (ν/θ)​(κr/B)(\nu/\theta)(\kappa_{r}/\sqrt{B}) grows with rr, reaching ∼11%{\sim}11\% at r=24r=24 (Table 1), which accounts for the majority of the observed discrepancy. The barrier-aware refinement (12) closes this gap in throughput estimation; in the present configuration, both rules agree on the simulation-optimal r∗r^{*}, indicating that the closed-form mean-field rule already provides accurate provisioning under typical operating conditions.

Figure 3 (right) presents the idle ratios for Attention (ηA\eta_{A}) and FFN (ηF\eta_{F}) instances. When rr is small, FFN completes quickly and idles while waiting for Attention outputs (ηF>60%\eta_{F}>60\% at r=1r=1). As rr increases, more Attention instances feed the shared FFN, improving its utilization.

5.4 Ablation Studies on Workload and Configuration Parameters

We now investigate how the optimal A/F ratio r∗r^{*} varies with key system parameters: microbatch size BB, decode length distribution parameter pp, and prefill length distribution parameter qq.

Ablation on Batch Size BB. Figure 4(a) compares throughput across three batch sizes (B∈{128,256,512}B\in\{128,256,512\}) with corresponding theoretical optimal ratios r∗={7.08,9.34,10.31}r^{*}=\{7.08,9.34,10.31\}. The results demonstrate that larger batch sizes achieve higher peak throughput: batching amortizes fixed overhead costs across more requests, thereby improving hardware utilization. Meanwhile, the optimal r∗r^{*} increases moderately with BB, as larger batches require more Attention instances to fully saturate the shared FFN server.

Ablation on Workload Distribution. Figure 4(b) examines the impact of prefill and decode length distribution. The results reveals that the optimal r∗r^{*} scales with total context length. Both longer prefills (μP\mu_{P}) and longer decode sequences (μD\mu_{D}) increase the total token load in the KV cache, placing greater computational pressure on the Attention side. Consequently, more Attention instances are required to balance the shared FFN server.

Appendix A Supplementary Materials for Section 4

A.1 Proof of Lemma 4.1

We use the discrete-time renewal-reward theorem applied to one decode slot. Each request constitutes one renewal cycle. Cycle nn has length DnD_{n} steps, during which the slot visits ages a=0,1,…,Dn−1a=0,1,\ldots,D_{n}-1. For any measurable function g⁡(P,a)g(P,a) with 𝔼⁡[∑a=0D−1|g⁡(P,a)|]<∞\mathbb{E}[\sum_{a=0}^{D-1}|g(P,a)|]<\infty, the renewal-reward theorem gives the long-run time average

𝔼π​[g⁡(P,A)]=𝔼⁡[∑a=0D−1g⁡(P,a)]𝔼⁡[D],\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[g(P,A)]=\frac{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{a=0}^{D-1}g(P,a)\right]}{\mathbb{E}[D]}, (13)

where AA denotes the stationary age and the expectation on the right is taken over a single cycle.

First moment.

Take g⁡(P,a)=P+ag(P,a)=P+a. Using ∑a=0D−1(P+a)=D​P+D⁡(D−1)/2\sum_{a=0}^{D-1}(P+a)=DP+D(D-1)/2,

θ=𝔼π​[P+A]=𝔼⁡[D​P+D⁡(D−1)/2]𝔼⁡[D],\theta=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[P+A]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[DP+D(D-1)/2]}{\mathbb{E}[D]},

which proves the first identity in (3). Condition 𝔼⁡[D]<∞\mathbb{E}[D]<\infty together with (2) ensures the integrability required by (13).

Second moment.

Take g⁡(P,a)=(P+a)2g(P,a)=(P+a)^{2}. Expanding and using ∑a=0D−11=D\sum_{a=0}^{D-1}1=D, ∑a=0D−1a=D⁡(D−1)/2\sum_{a=0}^{D-1}a=D(D-1)/2, and ∑a=0D−1a2=D⁡(D−1)​(2​D−1)/6\sum_{a=0}^{D-1}a^{2}=D(D-1)(2D-1)/6,

∑a=0D−1(P+a)2=D​P2+P​D​(D−1)+D​(D−1)​(2​D−1)6.\sum_{a=0}^{D-1}(P+a)^{2}=DP^{2}+PD(D-1)+\frac{D(D-1)(2D-1)}{6}.

Substituting into (13) proves the second identity in (3), and ν2=𝔼⁡[Y2]−θ2\nu^{2}=\mathbb{E}[Y^{2}]-\theta^{2}.

Independent case.

If P⟂⟂DP\perp\!\!\!\perp D, then 𝔼⁡[D​P]/𝔼⁡[D]=μP\mathbb{E}[DP]/\mathbb{E}[D]=\mu_{P} and

𝔼⁡[D⁡(D−1)]2​𝔼​[D]=μD2+σD2−μD2​μD=μD−12+σD22​μD,\frac{\mathbb{E}[D(D-1)]}{2\mathbb{E}[D]}=\frac{\mu_{D}^{2}+\sigma_{D}^{2}-\mu_{D}}{2\mu_{D}}=\frac{\mu_{D}-1}{2}+\frac{\sigma_{D}^{2}}{2\mu_{D}},

which proves (4). Without independence, 𝔼⁡[D​P]/𝔼⁡[D]=μP+Cov⁡(P,D)/μD\mathbb{E}[DP]/\mathbb{E}[D]=\mu_{P}+\mathrm{Cov}(P,D)/\mu_{D}, giving the additional covariance term. □\square

Assume ν>0\nu>0 (the case ν=0\nu=0 is immediate, since Yj,b=θY_{j,b}=\theta a.s. implies WB,r=B​θW_{B,r}=B\theta exactly). Define

Xj(B):=Tj(B)−B​θB​ν,j=1,…,r.X_{j}^{(B)}:=\frac{T_{j}^{(B)}-B\theta}{\sqrt{B}\,\nu},\qquad j=1,\ldots,r.

A.3 Monte Carlo Validation of the Barrier Approximation

We validate Theorem 4.3 by comparing the predicted relative synchronization overhead κr​s/m\kappa_{r}s/m against Monte Carlo (MC) estimates. The experiment uses geometric decode lifetimes (Corollary 4.5) with B=256B=256, μP=100\mu_{P}=100, μD=500\mu_{D}=500. Each worker’s token load sums BB independent slot loads, giving Tj≈𝒩⁡(m,s2)T_{j}\approx\mathcal{N}(m,s^{2}) with m=B⁡(μP+μD)m=B(\mu_{P}+\mu_{D}) and s=B⁡(σP2+μD​(μD+1))s=\sqrt{B(\sigma_{P}^{2}+\mu_{D}(\mu_{D}+1))}. MC estimates use 50,00050{,}000 independent trials per value of rr.

The CLT prediction matches the MC estimate within 0.5%0.5\% across all tested values of rr, confirming the accuracy of the Gaussian order-statistic approximation.

A.4 Derivation of the Gaussian Cycle Time (9)

We show that τ¯​(B,r)=τG​(B,r)+o⁡(B)\bar{\tau}(B;r)=\tau_{G}(B;r)+o(\sqrt{B}), where τG\tau_{G} is defined in (9).

τ¯​(B,r)=GB,r+σA​𝔼​[(XB−zB,r)+].\bar{\tau}(B;r)=G_{B,r}+\sigma_{A}\mathbb{E}[(X_{B}-z_{B,r})_{+}]. (14)

We claim 𝔼⁡[(XB−zB,r)+]−𝔼⁡[(Mr−zB,r)+]→0\mathbb{E}[(X_{B}-z_{B,r})_{+}]-\mathbb{E}[(M_{r}-z_{B,r})_{+}]\to 0 as B→∞B\to\infty.

The map x↦(x−z)+x\mapsto(x-z)_{+} is continuous with linear growth; weak convergence XB⇒MrX_{B}\Rightarrow M_{r} together with uniform L2L^{2}-boundedness (supB𝔼⁡[XB2]≤r\sup_{B}\mathbb{E}[X_{B}^{2}]\leq r) yields 𝔼⁡[(XB−z)+]→𝔼⁡[(Mr−z)+]\mathbb{E}[(X_{B}-z)_{+}]\to\mathbb{E}[(M_{r}-z)_{+}], and Lipschitz continuity in zz extends the conclusion to zB,r→zz_{B,r}\to z.

Case 2: zB,r→+∞z_{B,r}\to+\infty. Cauchy–Schwarz and Markov’s inequality give 𝔼⁡[(XB−zB,r)+]≤𝔼⁡[XB2]/zB,r→0\mathbb{E}[(X_{B}-z_{B,r})_{+}]\leq\mathbb{E}[X_{B}^{2}]/z_{B,r}\to 0, and similarly for MrM_{r}.

Case 3: zB,r→−∞z_{B,r}\to-\infty. Write (XB−zB,r)+=(XB−zB,r)−(XB−zB,r)−(X_{B}-z_{B,r})_{+}=(X_{B}-z_{B,r})-(X_{B}-z_{B,r})_{-}. In all three cases, the difference vanishes. Substituting into (14) and using the density fMr​(m)=r​ϕ​(m)​Φ​(m)r−1f_{M_{r}}(m)=r\phi(m)\Phi(m)^{r-1} to evaluate 𝔼⁡[(Mr−zB,r)+]\mathbb{E}[(M_{r}-z_{B,r})_{+}] as the integral in (9) completes the proof. □\square

Closed form for small rr.

For r=1r=1, M1∼𝒩⁡(0,1)M_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) and the integral in (9) reduces to ϕ⁡(z)−z⁡(1−Φ⁡(z))\phi(z)-z(1-\Phi(z)) at z=zB,1z=z_{B,1}. For r=2r=2, the integral admits a closed form in terms of ϕ\phi, Φ\Phi, and Owen’s TT-function. For r≥3r\geq 3, numerical quadrature is straightforward.

Recall

GB,r=max⁡{αC​B​r+βC,αF​B​r+βF},τmf​(B,r)=max⁡{μA,GB,r}.G_{B,r}=\max\{\alpha_{C}Br+\beta_{C},\alpha_{F}Br+\beta_{F}\},\qquad\tau_{\mathrm{mf}}(B;r)=\max\{\mu_{A},G_{B,r}\}.

which is increasing in rr. This region ends at

min⁡{μA−βCαC​B,μA−βFαF​B}.\min\!\left\{\frac{\mu_{A}-\beta_{C}}{\alpha_{C}B},\frac{\mu_{A}-\beta_{F}}{\alpha_{F}B}\right\}.

dd​r​log⁡r​B(r+1)​(αi​B​r+βi)=βi−αi​B​r2r⁡(r+1)​(αi​B​r+βi).\frac{d}{dr}\log\frac{rB}{(r+1)(\alpha_{i}Br+\beta_{i})}=\frac{\beta_{i}-\alpha_{i}Br^{2}}{r(r+1)(\alpha_{i}Br+\beta_{i})}.

Thus the only smooth stationary points are

βCαC​B,βFαF​B.\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{C}}{\alpha_{C}B}},\qquad\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{F}}{\alpha_{F}B}}.

The only nonsmooth point is the crossing of the communication and FFN latencies,

Therefore the global optimum must be one of the candidates in (10); choosing the one with the largest Thrmf​(B,r)\mathrm{Thr}_{\mathrm{mf}}(B;r) gives rmf∗r^{*}_{\mathrm{mf}}. Substitution gives the stated optimal throughput. □\square

A.6 Trace-Based Nonparametric Estimator

Given a request trace (Pi,Di)i=1n(P_{i},D_{i})_{i=1}^{n}, the framework requires no parametric model. Estimate θ\theta and the second moment of YY by

θ^\displaystyle\hat{\theta} =∑i=1n[Di​Pi+Di​(Di−1)/2]∑i=1nDi,\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[D_{i}P_{i}+D_{i}(D_{i}-1)/2\big]}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}}, (15)
q^\displaystyle\hat{q} =∑i=1n[Di​Pi2+Pi​Di​(Di−1)+Di​(Di−1)​(2​Di−1)/6]∑i=1nDi,\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[D_{i}P_{i}^{2}+P_{i}D_{i}(D_{i}-1)+D_{i}(D_{i}-1)(2D_{i}-1)/6\big]}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}}, (16)

and set ν^2=q^−θ^2\hat{\nu}^{2}=\hat{q}-\hat{\theta}^{2}. Both estimators are ratios of i.i.d. sums and are strongly consistent under the moment conditions of Lemma 4.1. A standard delta-method argument gives n\sqrt{n}-asymptotic normality under the additional condition that the corresponding cycle-reward variables have finite second moments. Plugging (θ^,ν^)(\hat{\theta},\hat{\nu}) into Theorems 4.4 and the barrier-aware rule (12) yields the empirical provisioning rule, computable directly from serving logs.

A.7 Heavy-Tailed Decode Lifetimes

The finite-variance Theorem 4.3 requires ν2<∞\nu^{2}<\infty. Because the stationary age distribution is length-biased, this is stronger than finite variance of DD. If ℙ⁡(D>x)∼C​x−α\mathbb{P}(D>x)\sim Cx^{-\alpha}, the stationary age AA has tail

ℙ⁡(A>x)=∑a>xℙ⁡(D>a)𝔼⁡[D]∼C𝔼​[D]​(α−1)​x−(α−1),\mathbb{P}(A>x)=\frac{\sum_{a>x}\mathbb{P}(D>a)}{\mathbb{E}[D]}\sim\frac{C}{\mathbb{E}[D](\alpha-1)}\,x^{-(\alpha-1)},

shifting the tail exponent from α\alpha to α−1\alpha-1. Consequently:

  • •

    α>3\alpha>3: ν2<∞\nu^{2}<\infty, and Theorem 4.3 applies.

  • •

    2<α≤32<\alpha\leq 3: θ<∞\theta<\infty but ν2=∞\nu^{2}=\infty. The Gaussian B\sqrt{B} correction is replaced by stable-law fluctuations; if YY lies in the domain of attraction of a γ\gamma-stable law with γ=α−1\gamma=\alpha-1, then WB,r=B​θ+B1/γ​𝔼​[max1≤j≤r⁡Sj]+o⁡(B1/γ)W_{B,r}=B\theta+B^{1/\gamma}\,\mathbb{E}[\max_{1\leq j\leq r}S_{j}]+o(B^{1/\gamma}) for i.i.d. γ\gamma-stable SjS_{j}.

  • •

    α≤2\alpha\leq 2: θ\theta may be infinite; the mean-field token load is undefined.

In practice, serving systems impose maximum context and generation lengths, restoring all moments, so condition (2) is satisfied.

Appendix B Supplementary Materials for Section 5

This appendix presents the methodology for deriving the latency model parameters αA,βA,αF,βF,αC,βC\alpha_{A},\beta_{A},\alpha_{F},\beta_{F},\alpha_{C},\beta_{C} used in the main text. We demonstrate the derivation process using the DeepSeek-V3 architecture, but the methodology generalizes to other models and hardware platforms.

Note on hardware parameters.

Due to confidentiality constraints, we cannot disclose the explicit Huawei Ascend 910C hardware specifications used in our experiments. Instead, we present the derivation framework using symbolic hardware parameters (summarized in Table 2), enabling practitioners to apply this methodology to their own hardware platforms. The final parameter values in Table 3 were obtained via linear regression on real execution traces over Huawei Ascend 910C.

B.1 Model Configuration

We base our derivations on the DeepSeek-V3 architecture. The model has a hidden size of H=7168H=7168 and uses Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a compressed KV cache dimension of (dc+drope)=512+64=576(d_{c}+d_{\mathrm{rope}})=512+64=576. For the MoE layers, the expert intermediate dimension is dexpert=2048d_{\mathrm{expert}}=2048, with a total of Nexpert=256N_{\mathrm{expert}}=256 experts across the system, where each token is routed to k=8k=8 experts. We use Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) with depth 1.

B.2 MLA Attention (Memory-Bound)

During decoding, Attention computation is memory-bound, dominated by reading the compressed KV cache from HBM. The compute cost scales with total token load T=∑b=1B(sb+ib)T=\sum_{b=1}^{B}(s_{b}+i_{b}).

B.2.1 Derivation

Data volume per token.

With KV compression dimension (dc+drope)=576(d_{c}+d_{\mathrm{rope}})=576 and BF16 precision (2 bytes per element):

Vtoken=(dc+drope)×2=576×2=1152​bytes.V_{\mathrm{token}}=(d_{c}+d_{\mathrm{rope}})\times 2=576\times 2=1152~\text{bytes}. (17)
Effective HBM bandwidth.

Accounting for non-coalesced memory access patterns, cache effects, and memory controller overhead, the effective bandwidth is:

βeff=βHBM×ηmem.\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}=\beta_{\mathrm{HBM}}\times\eta_{\mathrm{mem}}. (18)
Time per token (slope).

The per-token memory access time gives the slope parameter:

αA=Vtokenβeff=(dc+drope)×2βHBM×ηmem.\alpha_{A}=\frac{V_{\mathrm{token}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{eff}}}=\frac{(d_{c}+d_{\mathrm{rope}})\times 2}{\beta_{\mathrm{HBM}}\times\eta_{\mathrm{mem}}}. (19)
Fixed overhead (intercept).

The intercept βA\beta_{A} captures the other projections in the attention block, including Query/Key/Value/Output projections in memory-bound status as well as vector operations such as RMSNorm or RoPE. This parameter is best determined empirically via profiling or linear regression on execution traces.

B.3 MoE FFN (Compute-Bound)

The FFN computation is compute-bound when batch size is sufficiently large. Let BeB_{e} denote the batch size per expert.

B.3.1 Derivation

FLOPs per expert.

For SwiGLU activation with 3 weight matrices (quantized gate, up, down projections):

FLOPs per expert=6×H×dexpert×Be=6×7168×2048×Be≈8.81×107×Be.\text{FLOPs per expert}=6\times H\times d_{\mathrm{expert}}\times B_{e}=6\times 7168\times 2048\times B_{e}\approx 8.81\times 10^{7}\times B_{e}. (20)
Effective compute throughput.

For MoE workloads with dynamic routing and load imbalance, the effective throughput is:

πeff=πpeak×ηcompute.\pi_{\mathrm{eff}}=\pi_{\mathrm{peak}}\times\eta_{\mathrm{compute}}. (21)
Compute time per expert.
texpert​(Be)=6×H×dexpert×Beπeff=6×H×dexpertπpeak×ηcompute⋅Be.t_{\text{expert}}(B_{e})=\frac{6\times H\times d_{\mathrm{expert}}\times B_{e}}{\pi_{\mathrm{eff}}}=\frac{6\times H\times d_{\mathrm{expert}}}{\pi_{\mathrm{peak}}\times\eta_{\mathrm{compute}}}\cdot B_{e}. (22)
Total FFN time per card.

With Nexpert/cardN_{\mathrm{expert/card}} experts per card:

tFFN,card​(Be)=Nexpert/card×texpert​(Be)+βoverhead.t_{\text{FFN,card}}(B_{e})=N_{\mathrm{expert/card}}\times t_{\text{expert}}(B_{e})+\beta_{\text{overhead}}. (23)
Batch size mapping.

The relationship between global batch BFB_{F} and batch per expert BeB_{e}:

Be=BF×k×(1+MTP depth)Nexpert=BF×8×2256=BF16.B_{e}=\frac{B_{F}\times k\times(1+\text{MTP depth})}{N_{\mathrm{expert}}}=\frac{B_{F}\times 8\times 2}{256}=\frac{B_{F}}{16}. (24)
Express in terms of global batch.

Substituting the batch size mapping, the FFN latency takes the form:

tF​(BF)=αF⋅BF+βF,t_{F}(B_{F})=\alpha_{F}\cdot B_{F}+\beta_{F}, (25)

where:

αF=Nexpert/card×6×H×dexpertπpeak×ηcompute×k×(1+MTP depth)Nexpert.\alpha_{F}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{expert/card}}\times 6\times H\times d_{\mathrm{expert}}}{\pi_{\mathrm{peak}}\times\eta_{\mathrm{compute}}}\times\frac{k\times(1+\text{MTP depth})}{N_{\mathrm{expert}}}. (26)

B.4 Communication

Communication involves transferring activations between Attention and FFN instances via high-speed interconnects.

B.4.1 Derivation

Data volume per batch.

For a batch of BeB_{e} tokens routed to experts, the activation transfer includes input (factor of 1 with INT8 format) and output (factor of 2 with BF16 format) tokens:

Vcomm​(Be)=3×H×Be=3×7168×Be=21504×Be​bytes.V_{\mathrm{comm}}(B_{e})=3\times H\times B_{e}=3\times 7168\times B_{e}=21504\times B_{e}~\text{bytes}. (27)
Effective network bandwidth.

For the AFD topology spanning both intra-node and inter-node communication, the effective aggregated bandwidth depends on the network topology and routing:

βnet=f⁡(βintra,βinter,topology),\beta_{\mathrm{net}}=f(\beta_{\mathrm{intra}},\beta_{\mathrm{inter}},\text{topology}), (28)

where the function ff depends on the specific deployment configuration.

Transfer time.
tcomm​(Be)=Ne​x​p​e​r​t/c​a​r​d​Vcomm​(Be)βnet+βC=3×Hβnet⋅Be+βC.t_{\mathrm{comm}}(B_{e})=\frac{N_{expert/card}V_{\mathrm{comm}}(B_{e})}{\beta_{\mathrm{net}}}+\beta_{C}=\frac{3\times H}{\beta_{\mathrm{net}}}\cdot B_{e}+\beta_{C}. (29)
Convert to per-token formulation.

With batch size mapping Be=BF/16B_{e}=B_{F}/16, the communication latency becomes:

tC​(r​B)=αC⋅r​B+βC,t_{C}(rB)=\alpha_{C}\cdot rB+\beta_{C}, (30)

where:

αC=Ne​x​p​e​r​t/c​a​r​d×3×Hβnet×k×(1+MTP depth)Nexpert.\alpha_{C}=N_{expert/card}\times\frac{3\times H}{\beta_{\mathrm{net}}}\times\frac{k\times(1+\text{MTP depth})}{N_{\mathrm{expert}}}. (31)

B.5 Summary

The derivations above provide a general framework for computing latency parameters from hardware specifications and model architecture. The key relationships are:

  • •

    Attention (memory-bound): αA∝dc+dropeβHBM×ηmem\alpha_{A}\propto\dfrac{d_{c}+d_{\mathrm{rope}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{HBM}}\times\eta_{\mathrm{mem}}}

  • •

    FFN (compute-bound): αF∝H×dexpertπpeak×ηcompute\alpha_{F}\propto\dfrac{H\times d_{\mathrm{expert}}}{\pi_{\mathrm{peak}}\times\eta_{\mathrm{compute}}}

  • •

    Communication: αC∝Hβnet\alpha_{C}\propto\dfrac{H}{\beta_{\mathrm{net}}}

Table 3 presents the parameter values used in our experiments. These values were obtained via linear regression on real execution traces collected from Huawei Ascend 910C NPUs, which provides empirical validation of the linear latency models while accounting for system-level effects not captured in first-principles analysis.

We visualize the derived latency models in Figure 6, which illustrates how Attention, FFN, and communication latencies scale with their respective input sizes under the parameters in Table 3.

Appendix C Compute resources.

All simulator experiments reported in Figures 3–4 and Appendix A.3 are CPU-only and do not require access to NPUs or GPUs once the latency coefficients are fixed. We ran the simulator on [CPU model] with [number] CPU cores and [RAM] memory. A single fan-in sweep for Figure 3 takes approximately 15 minutes, the batch-size and workload ablations in Figure 4 take approximately 20 minutes in total, and reproducing all reported simulator figures takes approximately 3 CPU-hours. The only accelerator-dependent component is the offline latency calibration used to obtain Table 3. These calibration traces were collected on Huawei Ascend 910C NPUs; raw profiling traces and detailed hardware parameters cannot be released due to confidentiality constraints, so reproduction of the paper’s simulator results uses the released fitted coefficients.
